title: Sort Characters By Frequency
description: Brute force to optimized: repeated rescanning versus a single sort versus bucket sort by frequency.

blocks.text: Given a string s, sort its characters in decreasing order based on how frequently each one appears, and return the resulting string.

blocks.caption: Bucket distinct characters by frequency, then rebuild by scanning from the highest bucket down

blocks.text: Given a string s, sort its characters in decreasing order based on how frequently each one appears, and return the resulting string.

blocks.title: Analogy: Arranging a Bowl of Mixed Candy by How Common Each Color Is
blocks.text: Like sorting a bowl of mixed colored candy so that whichever color appears the most sits at the front, and the least common colors sit toward the back, without needing the colors within one frequency group to follow any particular order.

blocks.caption: Rearrange the string so the most frequent characters come first

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["e appears twice, t and r each appear once","e should come first","e has a strictly higher frequency (2) than either t or r (1 each), so it must be placed before them"],["Answer","\"eert\" (or \"eetr\"), either grouping of the two e characters together is valid","Both orderings correctly place the two e's before the single t and single r; the tie between t and r can go either way"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["c and a both appear exactly 3 times, tied in frequency","either order between them is acceptable","Since neither character's frequency is strictly higher, the problem does not require one to precede the other"],["Answer","\"cccaaa\" (or \"aaaccc\")","Both orderings correctly group each character's occurrences together with no lower-frequency character interrupting them"]]}

blocks.text: Uppercase and lowercase letters are treated as distinct characters, so "A" and "a" are counted separately; "b" appears twice and is the most frequent, giving an answer like "bbAa" or "bbaA".

Before repeatedly hunting for the current maximum frequency, notice this problem asks for a full reordering by frequency, and "reorder everything by some key" is exactly what sorting, or bucketing when the key has a bounded range, is built for.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The final answer only depends on each distinct character's total frequency, never on where in the original string it appeared, so the problem reduces to: count frequencies, decide an order among distinct characters, then expand each one back out by its count.

Observation 2: Repeatedly scanning all remaining distinct characters to find the current highest frequency, one round per character, redoes almost the same comparison work over and over, since most characters' relative order does not actually change between rounds.

Observation 3: Sorting the distinct character-count pairs by count, descending, in one single sort call establishes the exact same final order in one pass instead of many separate rescans.

Observation 4: Because frequency itself can never exceed the length of s, exactly the same bucket-by-frequency trick used in Top K Frequent Elements applies here too: place each distinct character into a bucket by its frequency, then read the buckets off from highest to lowest, skipping the sort's comparisons entirely.

Whenever a problem asks to reorder distinct items by a frequency, or any other bounded-range, key, look past repeated max-finding toward a single sort, and further toward bucket sort if that key's range is small and known.

This problem and Top K Frequent Elements share the exact same underlying insight, just with a different final step: there, the top k values are read off; here, every character is expanded back out by its count to rebuild the full string.

Count every character's frequency, then repeatedly scan the remaining frequency counts to find whichever character currently has the highest count, append it that many times to the result, and remove it from consideration, repeating until every character has been placed.

items: Count the frequency of every character.
Repeatedly find the character with the highest remaining frequency by rescanning all remaining counts.
Append that character to the result its full count number of times, then remove it from further consideration.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: remaining starts as a separate copy of counts, since characters need to be removed from consideration as they are placed, while the original counts data is left available if needed elsewhere.
The search for the current maximum only considers what remains, not the original full set, since already-placed characters must not be reconsidered.
The best character is appended repeated exactly its own frequency number of times in one step, rather than appending it one character at a time in an inner loop.

blocks.text: Repeatedly picking the currently highest remaining frequency character correctly builds the string in strictly decreasing frequency order.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times d), where d is the number of distinct characters, since every round rescans all remaining distinct characters.
Space: O(d), for the frequency maps.

Limitation: rescanning all remaining distinct characters on every single round to find the current maximum is wasteful, when sorting the distinct characters by frequency just once up front achieves the same ordering directly.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force's repeated rescanning wastes effort re-deriving almost the same relative ordering information every single round, since removing the current maximum rarely changes how the remaining characters compare to each other. A single sort call establishes every character's final relative position all at once, using the exact same comparison information the repeated rescans were rediscovering piecemeal. Instead of many rounds of a rescan each, a single sort of the distinct characters produces the identical final order in one pass.

Count every character's frequency once. Then sort the distinct (character, count) pairs directly by count in descending order, a single sort call instead of repeated rescans. Finally, build the result by repeating each character its count times, in that sorted order.
Count once, sort the distinct pairs once, then rebuild the string in that order.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Count characters","t:1, r:1, e:2","A single pass over s tallies every character's total frequency before any ordering decision is made"],["Sort distinct pairs by count descending","(e,2), (t,1), (r,1), or (r,1) before (t,1), either tie order is fine","e's frequency of 2 is strictly greater than t and r's frequency of 1 each, so e must be placed first; t and r are tied and may appear in either order"],["Rebuild by repeating each character its count","\"ee\" + \"t\" + \"r\" = \"eetr\"","Expanding each distinct character back out by its own frequency, in the sorted order, reconstructs a valid answer string"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: count once, sort the distinct pairs once, then rebuild

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n plus d log d), one pass to count plus a single sort of the distinct characters.
Space: O(d), for the counts and the sorted list.

Sorting the distinct characters by their associated frequency in descending order establishes exactly the relative ordering the problem requires: any character with a strictly higher frequency than another is guaranteed to be placed before it, and characters with equal frequency may land in either relative order, which the problem explicitly permits. Expanding each character back out to its own frequency count, in that sorted order, reconstructs a string where every character's occurrences are grouped together and ordered correctly by frequency.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Comparison result","Placement"],"rows":[["One character's count is greater than another's","The higher-frequency character is placed first"],["Two characters' counts are equal","Either relative order is acceptable, since the problem does not constrain ties"]]}

items: The sort is applied only to the distinct characters, not every occurrence in the original string, since repeated occurrences of the same character all share one frequency and one position in the final order.
Expanding each character back to its full repeated form happens directly during the final join, without a separate explicit loop to build up the result string.
No frequency information is needed once the sort is complete, other than to know how many times to repeat each character during the final rebuild.

blocks.text: 10. Further Optimization: Bucket Sort by Frequency

Since frequency can never exceed the length of s, place each distinct character directly into a bucket indexed by its frequency, then scan the buckets from the highest frequency down, appending each character its count times as they are encountered. This avoids sorting entirely.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Bucket (frequency)","Characters here"],"rows":[["bucket 2","[e]"],["bucket 1","[t, r] (in whatever order they were counted)"]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: bucket characters by frequency, scan from the highest bucket down

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), counting and bucketing in linear passes, with no sorting.
Space: O(n), for the buckets.

items: The buckets array allocates one bucket per possible frequency, from 0 up to the maximum conceivable frequency of the string's own length, every character in s being the same one.
Each distinct character is placed directly into its frequency's bucket in O(1), with no comparison against any other character needed.
The final scan runs from the highest possible frequency down to 1, skipping bucket 0 entirely, since every distinct character present in s has a frequency of at least 1.

Each bucketed character is expanded back out to its full repeated form as the buckets are scanned, identical in spirit to the sorted version's rebuild step, just fed by bucket order instead of sort order.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (repeated max rescans)","O(n times d)","O(d)","Every one of d rounds rescans all remaining distinct characters"],["Optimized (single sort by frequency)","O(n plus d log d)","O(d)","One pass to count, one sort of the distinct characters, one rebuild pass"],["Further optimized (bucket sort by frequency)","O(n)","O(n)","No comparisons at all; frequency's bounded range (0 to n) allows direct bucket placement"]]}

blocks.text: This problem is a direct sibling of Top K Frequent Elements, sharing the same bucket sort by frequency trick, since frequency being bounded by the input length is what allows sorting to be replaced entirely by a linear bucketing pass.

items: Repeatedly rescanning remaining counts to find the current maximum instead of sorting once or bucketing, which unnecessarily multiplies the work by the number of distinct characters.
Forgetting that uppercase and lowercase letters are distinct characters and must be counted separately; silently merging "A" and "a" into one count would misorder the result.

Sorting the entire original string by frequency, character by character, instead of sorting only the smaller set of distinct characters and then expanding, which does unnecessary extra comparison work.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["A string where every character is distinct","Produces a tie in frequency across the board, where any relative order among them is acceptable"],["A single character string","Trivially returns itself, since there is nothing else to compare it against"]]}

items: Explicitly connect this problem to Top K Frequent Elements, since recognizing the shared "frequency is bounded by n, so bucket sort applies" insight across both problems demonstrates pattern recognition, not just memorized solutions.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Rearrange or sort elements by frequency" points toward counting once, then either sorting the distinct elements by count, or, if the count is bounded by a known small range, bucket sorting by count directly.

items: How is this different from Top K Frequent Elements, given they share the same bucket sort trick? There, only the top k values are read off from the buckets; here, every character must be expanded back out by its own frequency to rebuild the complete original-length string.

What if ties needed to be broken by a secondary rule, such as alphabetical order among equally frequent characters? Each bucket, or the sort's comparator, would need a secondary tie-breaking key, comparing characters directly whenever their frequencies are equal.

How would you handle a very large alphabet, such as full Unicode, instead of a small fixed character set? The bucket sort by frequency still works unchanged, since it buckets by frequency value, not by character identity, and frequency remains bounded by the string length regardless of alphabet size.
Direct sibling of Top K Frequent Elements, sharing the identical "frequency is bounded by n, so bucket sort applies" insight.
Same hash map frequency counting foundation as Ransom Note, Word Pattern, and Contains Duplicate, just paired here with a full reordering step instead of a comparison or lookup.
Same "sort once instead of repeatedly finding the current max" insight as any selection-sort-style algorithm being replaced by a single upfront sort.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n times d) time, O(d) space.
Optimized (sort distinct pairs by frequency): O(n plus d log d) time, O(d) space.
Further optimized (bucket sort by frequency): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Frequency counting followed by ordering distinct characters by frequency, refined from repeated rescans to a single sort to bucket sort
Core Idea: Since frequency is bounded by the string's own length, bucketing distinct characters by frequency and scanning from the highest bucket down avoids sorting entirely
Time: O(n) for the bucket sort version, O(n plus d log d) for the single-sort version
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Reordering by a bounded-range key, frequency capped at n, can always be done in linear time via bucket sort, instead of paying a comparison sort's log factor
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Same trick as Top K Frequent: bucket by frequency, then expand instead of just reading off
